title: QUIC & HTTP/3
summary: Why the web moved its transport onto UDP, and what QUIC and HTTP/3 actually change versus HTTP/2.

slides.markdown:
HTTP/3 is HTTP/2's semantics carried over a new transport: **QUIC**, built on UDP instead of TCP. The motivation isn't cosmetic — TCP itself has a head-of-line blocking flaw HTTP/2 couldn't route around, so the fix meant replacing the transport layer, not just the HTTP framing.

- QUIC reimplements reliability, ordering, and congestion control — the things TCP normally provides — on top of UDP.
- Streams are now independent even at the transport layer, not just the HTTP layer.
- TLS 1.3 is built into the handshake, not layered on afterward.

slides.subTitle: Transport-layer HOL blocking
slides.markdown:
HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one TCP connection, but TCP delivers bytes in **strict order**. Lose one segment, and the OS won't hand *any* later bytes to the application — even ones belonging to a completely different, unaffected HTTP/2 stream — until the lost segment is retransmitted. See [http2-multiplexing](http2-multiplexing) and [tcp-reliability-flow-control](tcp-reliability-flow-control).

That's **transport-layer head-of-line blocking**: a problem HTTP/2 can't fix from above, because ordering is enforced inside TCP itself, invisible to the application.

QUIC's core move: keep UDP's simplicity but rebuild everything TCP used to give — reliable delivery, ordering, congestion control — **inside QUIC itself, per stream**. Because QUIC owns this logic instead of the OS's TCP stack, a lost packet on one stream only blocks *that* stream's reassembly, not the whole connection.

This also means QUIC evolves independently of OS kernels: running in userspace over UDP, browsers and servers can ship transport improvements without waiting on OS updates.

![TCP: one lost segment stalls every multiplexed stream; QUIC: a lost packet only stalls its own stream](assets/quic-independent-streams.svg)

Because QUIC tracks loss and ordering **per stream** instead of per connection, streams 2 and 3 keep flowing the instant their packets arrive — stream 1's retransmit happens in parallel, invisible to the others. This is the fix HTTP/2 structurally couldn't make while sitting on top of TCP.

assets.alt: TCP: one lost segment stalls every multiplexed stream; QUIC: a lost packet only stalls its own stream

slides.markdown:
In TCP+TLS, encryption is a separate layer bolted on after the transport handshake: TCP's 3-way handshake completes, *then* the TLS handshake negotiates keys. QUIC folds them together — the **cryptographic and transport handshakes happen in the same round trip**, because QUIC was designed from the start assuming TLS 1.3.

A practical consequence: there's no such thing as unencrypted QUIC in normal deployment — encryption isn't optional or added later, it's structurally part of connection setup. See [tls-handshake-deep-dive](tls-handshake-deep-dive).

slides.subTitle: 0-RTT vs 1-RTT
slides.markdown:
| | TCP + TLS 1.3 | QUIC |
|---|---|---|
| First connection | 1 RTT (TCP) + 1 RTT (TLS) = 2 RTT | Combined into 1 RTT |
| Resumed connection | Still ≥1 RTT | **0-RTT** — data sent with the very first packet |
| What enables it | N/A — separate layers | Transport + crypto handshake unified |

**How to decide:** 0-RTT isn't free — data sent before the handshake completes is replayable by an attacker who captures it, so QUIC restricts 0-RTT to idempotent requests. It's a real win for repeat visitors, not a blanket "always faster" claim.

TCP identifies a connection by a 4-tuple (source/dest IP + port). Switch from Wi-Fi to cellular mid-session and your IP changes — TCP has no way to say "same connection, new address," so the connection dies and everything reconnects from scratch.

QUIC identifies a connection by a **connection ID** it generates, independent of IP/port. Switch networks mid-download, and QUIC just keeps going under the new IP — no reconnect, no restarted downloads. This matters directly for mobile: see [cellular-mobile-networking](cellular-mobile-networking).

slides.subTitle: HTTP semantics over QUIC
slides.markdown: HTTP/3 keeps the same HTTP semantics you already know — methods, status codes, headers (compressed with **QPACK**, HPACK's QUIC-safe cousin) — but carries them over QUIC streams instead of TCP. From an application-developer's perspective almost nothing changes: same requests, same responses. What changed is everything underneath: transport, loss recovery, and encryption are now QUIC's job, not TCP+TLS's.

![Round trips to first byte: TCP+TLS1.3+HTTP2 (2 RTT) vs QUIC+HTTP3 (1 RTT, or 0-RTT on resume)](assets/quic-handshake-rtt-comparison.svg)

Fewer round trips before the first useful byte matters most on high-latency links (mobile, long-distance) — shaving even one RTT off a 150ms round trip is a real, felt speedup on page load.

assets.alt: Round trips to first byte: TCP+TLS1.3+HTTP2 (2 RTT) vs QUIC+HTTP3 (1 RTT, or 0-RTT on resume)

slides.markdown:
| | HTTP/2 | HTTP/3 |
|---|---|---|
| Transport | TCP | QUIC (over UDP) |
| Header compression | HPACK | QPACK |
| Stream independence | App-layer only | Full — down to loss recovery |
| Connection survives IP change | No | Yes (connection ID) |
| Handshake | TCP + TLS (2 RTT) | QUIC (1 RTT, 0-RTT on resume) |

What stayed the same: HTTP methods, status codes, general request/response semantics, and most caching/header behavior — HTTP/3 is a transport swap, not a new HTTP model.

slides.subTitle: "Just HTTP/2 on UDP"
slides.markdown: A common shortcut: **"QUIC is just HTTP/2 running on UDP."** It isn't — QUIC redesigns loss recovery (per-stream instead of per-connection), congestion control (with more modern algorithms and better signaling than classic TCP), and folds in TLS 1.3 at the transport level. Treating it as a drop-in swap misses *why* it was built: fixing transport-layer HOL blocking and handshake latency, problems that live below where HTTP/2 could ever reach.
